title: The Fisherman and His Wife
text:
A poor fisherman lived with his wife Ilsebill in a miserable hovel by the sea. One day he caught a great flounder, which spoke to him: it was an enchanted prince, it said, and begged to be let go. The fisherman released it at once.

When he told his wife, she asked whether he had wished for anything. He had not. She sent him back to ask the fish for a little cottage. He went reluctantly, called the flounder, and the wish was granted. Soon the cottage was not enough. She sent him back for a stone castle, then to make her king, then emperor, then pope. Each time the fisherman went unwillingly, and each time the sea looked darker and more troubled, but each time the flounder said, "Go home, she already is."

Every evening the wife lay awake, unable to sleep for wanting more. At last, watching the sunrise, she declared that she wanted to be like God, so that she could make the sun and moon rise.

The fisherman went out into a raging storm, with waves as high as church towers, and shouted the wish to the flounder. "Go home," it said. "She is sitting in her old hovel again." And there they are still sitting to this day.
lesson: Wanting more is natural, but a household that is never satisfied can lose everything it already had. Learn to recognize enough.
people: The fisherman, his wife Ilsebill, the flounder
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 19 (Von dem Fischer un syner Fru), from Philipp Otto Runge's Low German version
